title: Does Air Quality Matter? Evidence from the Housing Market
research_question: Does air quality get capitalized into residential property values? Specifically, do reductions in ambient particulate matter concentrations cause increases in housing prices, and what is the magnitude of homeowners' willingness to pay for cleaner air?
data_description: The authors assemble county-level panel data covering U.S. counties over 1970-1990. Air pollution data on total suspended particulates (TSPs) come from the EPA's Air Quality Subsystem (AQS) database (obtained via FOIA), providing annual geometric means and percentile readings from monitors aggregated to the county level for 1971-1990. County attainment/non-attainment status for each year was hand-collected from the Code of Federal Regulations (Title 40, Part 80) for 1978-1990 and reconstructed from monitor readings and the federal selection rule for 1972-1977. Property value data (log median value of owner-occupied housing) and county characteristics (demographics, socioeconomics, crime, medical, fiscal/tax, housing structure) come from the 1972, 1983, and 1994 County and City Data Books and the 1980 and 1990 Census 5% PUMS. Monitored counties contain roughly 80-85% of the U.S. population.
institutional_context: Before 1970, federal involvement in air pollution control was minimal. The 1970 Clean Air Act Amendments established federal National Ambient Air Quality Standards applied at the county level for pollutants including total suspended particulates, with a TSP annual geometric mean ceiling of 75 μg/m³ and a 24-hour maximum of 260 μg/m³. Counties exceeding these thresholds were designated 'non-attainment'; others were 'attainment.' Non-attainment counties faced substantially stricter federal regulatory oversight: new and modified polluting sources had to install state-of-the-art abatement equipment, obtain permits, and offset emissions increases, while existing major stationary sources received emissions limits. Attainment counties faced much lighter requirements. The 1977 Amendments strengthened enforcement, made State Implementation Plans both state and federal law, and authorized EPA construction bans, civil and criminal penalties, and withholding of federal funds. This federally imposed, county-level discrete regulatory designation generated sharp differences in pollution-abatement pressure across otherwise similar counties.
